items.title: Bangladesh: Fair Trial Concerns at Tribunal
items.description: Click to expand Image Bangladesh military personnel guard the International Criminal Tribunal in Dhaka, Bangladesh, November 17, 2025. © 2025 Mamunur Rashid/NurPhoto via AP Photo (London) – Bangladesh authorities are failing to uphold international legal standards at the country’s International Crimes Tribunal, Human Rights Watch said today. The failures risk denying justice to victims, undermining the rule of law, falsely imprisoning political opponents, and repeating the rights violations of the past. On July 27, prosecutors submitted charges against 41 people for crimes against humanity and genocide. The tribunal is prosecuting individuals, including politicians, members of security forces, and even journalists, accused of serious human rights violations under former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League government, which was toppled by protests in 2024 after over 15 years of increasingly authoritarian rule. “Those responsible for the many abuses committed under the Sheikh Hasina government should be appropriately held to account, but many prosecutions are falling short of international fair trial standards,” said Meenakshi Ganguly, deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “Bangladesh needs to urgently reform its criminal justice system, and the new government should ensure that there is no room for political vendettas through shoddy investigations and arbitrary allegations.” The tribunal is hearing cases related to the security forces crackdown on student-led protests in July and August 2024, resulting in over 800 deaths and thousands of serious injuries, which ultimately toppled the Awami League government. The tribunal is also prosecuting other abuses, including alleged extrajudicial killings and disappearances, committed during Hasina’s rule. Human Rights Watch monitoring of over a dozen cases being prosecuted by the International Crimes Tribunal—a domestic tribunal mandated to try serious crimes under international law—raises significant concerns regarding due process. Prosecutors have detained and charged individuals for alleged crimes and in multiple cases relied on witness statements in which incriminating passages appear to have been cut and pasted into multiple statements. Since the fall of Hasina’s government, the tribunal has completed 6 trials, resulting in the conviction of 62 people for crimes against humanity; 42 were tried in absentia, including Hasina herself; and 16 were sentenced to death. The tribunal was first established by Hasina’s government in March 2010, to prosecute individuals who had allegedly committed crimes under international law, such as crimes against humanity, in support of the Pakistan military during Bangladesh’s 1971 war of independence. Those trials, which resulted in six executions, were widely criticized for lack of evidence, political bias, collusion between prosecutors and judges, and absence of basic due process protections. After Hasina’s government was toppled by protesters in 2024, an interim government amended the law governing the tribunal, altering the definition of offenses under its jurisdiction to comply with international standards. However, these amendments fell short of ensuring due process and procedural standards equivalent to international courts dealing with similar offenses, Human Rights Watch found. The current administration led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s Bangladesh Nationalist Party was elected in February 2026 and made no further amendments. The law governing the tribunal still allows prosecutors to order the arrest of individuals without meeting any evidential threshold, to hold detainees for months without written reasons for their detention, and to provide no right of interlocutory appeal to a separate court. Trials can begin three weeks after the prosecution discloses its evidence, leaving little time for adequate defense preparation. Trials in absentia are held without appropriate safeguards including defendants’ right to choose lawyers to represent them. And the tribunal restricts defense lawyers’ ability to cross-examine witnesses. On May 14, the tribunal ordered the arrest of two journalists for their reporting on a May 2013 protest by a fundamentalist group called Hefazat-e-Islam. While human rights groups had reported excessive use of force that killed several protesters, the prosecutors accused Mozammel Babu, managing director of Ekattor TV, a network that supported the then-Awami League government, and Farzana Rupa, a prominent presenter, of helping the government cover up the killings by presenting “false information.” The journalists’ lawyers told Human Rights Watch that the prosecutors did not provide either journalist with a written explanation of the grounds for their arrest, in breach of Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and as required by Bangladesh’s International Crimes (Tribunal) Act. On July 27, the prosecutors included the 2 journalists among 41 people listed in charges submitted to the Tribunal, accusing them of crimes against humanity, and also genocide. Under international law, genocide is defined as certain acts committed with the intent of destroying, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group as such. Human Rights Watch has found that tribunal prosecutors and judges are relying on statements recorded by investigating officers that contain passages duplicated across multiple statements, casting doubt on their authenticity. One example is the case of Dr. Muhammad Hasan Mahmud Chowdhury and others, in which the tribunal set out three charges against 22 Awami League politicians and activists over killings in Chittagong city center on July 16 and 18, and August 4, 2024. A key part of the prosecution’s evidence are 55 witness statements that have been made public. One six-line passage, which appears almost word-for-word in fourteen separate statements, claims that seven named politicians had through their “planning, financing, provocation and instructions” used “Awami League terrorists” to kill six people. A second, longer passage, which appears virtually identically in nine further statements, claims that six of the accused had repeatedly made “provocative statements,” branded the protesters “militants, terrorists, and communal agitators,” and instructed the sixteen other accused to “use maximum force to suppress the movement and explicitly ordered the killing and torture of innocent, unarmed, peaceful students and the public.” In this same case, the defense team for one of the 22 accused, ABM Fazle Karim Chowdhury, a senior Awami League politician who is in custody, provided journalists with recordings purportedly of a tribunal prosecutor offering to secure Karim’s bail earlier in the year in exchange for 10 million takas (US$82,000). The prosecutor resigned following the disclosure, but the chief prosecutor’s office has yet to complete its investigation, while the judges have proceeded with framing charges and the trial is due to start on August 6. “Bangladesh authorities need to recognize that they cannot repeat the abuses of the past, when the Awami League conducted political witch-hunts,” Ganguly said. “Allegations based on duplicated witness statements, however, show the lack of a credible justice process, which will once again fail victims, their families, and all Bangladeshis.”

items.title: Lack of access to cooling to amplify heat deaths in Pakistan
items.description: • 89pc of Pakistan’s population trapped in deadly combination of extreme heat, lack of access to air conditioning • Chicago University study says 377,000 lives projected to be lost each year by 2050, including 150,000 in Pakistan ISLAMABAD: As extreme heat events become more frequent, most poor countries lack the resources to power the cooling systems needed to adapt to rising temperatures, resulting in 10 times more deaths compared to their wealthier counterparts. According to a new study by the Climate Impact Lab , headquartered at the University of Chicago, climate-driven temperature changes are on track to cause about 430,000 more deaths annually by 2050, and cooling systems can play a major role in preventing these deaths. Areas in 18 countries—home to 676 million people— are trapped in a deadly combination of extreme heat and lack of cooling, described as a ‘mortality-cooling trap’ (MCT) by the study. As many as 377,000 lives are projected to be lost each year starting in 2050 due to warmer temperatures in these countries, including Pakistan, Nigar, Nepal etc. All of these people live in either low-income or lower middle-income countries today, mostly in northern sub-Saharan Africa such as Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso and Chad. The rest live in southern Asia, including Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal and Myanmar. The study noted that these countries will not be able to respond in the same way as richer countries due to energy affordability constraints. For instance, the projected increase in electricity use per person in Niger will be 1/9th that of Saudi Arabia, and communities in Niger will lose 27,000 more lives annually in 2050 due to a warmer climate than its wealthier counterpart. According to the study, the largest city in each MCT country by population, together accounting for more than 80 million people in their metro areas, all 18 of them are projected to see increases in electricity consumption that are below the global median, and 10 of them are also projected to experience significant net increases in temperature-related mortality. “Across the globe, more than 20 large cities exceed those same thresholds, with Pakistan (9 cities), Bangladesh (2 cities), and Sudan (2 cities) having the most, highlighting areas that will be hindered from adapting to heat via electricity-dependent interventions.” The report estimates that 89 per cent of Pakistan’s population could live in affected regions, with 57 additional temperature-related deaths per 100,000 people and a slight decline in climate-induced electricity consumption by mid-century. The deadly combination of extreme heat and lack of access to AC could lead to over 150,000 more deaths each year by 2050. “We’ve identified the places most at risk of seeing more people die from the heat and least able to power up ACs to save them, so people and governments can zero in on saving the greatest number of lives,” said Ashwin Rode, a fellow at the Climate Impact Lab and director of scientific research at the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC). Despite massive solar installations, adaptation for countries like Pakistan remains complicated. “Increasing access to electricity through renewable sources such as solar can be an important adaptation strategy and will definitely help. Yet the high cost of installing and running energy-intensive cooling technologies like AC will continue to keep it out of reach for large sections of the population,” Rode told Dawn. Earlier this year, the FBR chairman said that out of 42 million households, at least 7 per cent own air-conditioners in Pakistan, Nukta reported. ‘Unequal access to cooling’ According to energy expert Dr Khalid Waleed, Pakistan’s projected ‘mortality-cooling trap’ is not simply a shortage-of-electricity problem but fundamentally a problem of affordability, reliability and unequal access to cooling. He agreed with Rode, saying that the need for cooling may not translate into actual electricity consumption because many households cannot afford air conditioners, efficient fans or increasingly expensive electricity, while unreliable grids further constrain adaptation. “In economic terms, this is suppressed demand, not an absence of demand,” the expert noted. He said the abovementioned projection should be understood as a warning rather than an unavoidable outcome. “It is based on a middle-of-the-road development pathway, approximately 3°C of warming by 2100, and largely ‘status quo’ adaptation behaviour,” Dr Waleed said, adding that rapid shift towards distributed solar energy demonstrated that technological and policy changes could alter this trajectory despite some socioeconomic limitations. Similarly, the CIL report also suggested reforms in the power sector, early warning systems, heat action plans, and improved temperature forecasts for cities to adapt to heat. Dr Waleed, also a research fellow at Sustainable Policy Development Institute, agreed. Affordable electricity, resilient distribution networks, efficient cooling appliances, public cooling spaces, heat-health action plans, urban greening and targeted social protection must all be treated as essential climate-adaptation infrastructure, he said. “The real danger is not that electricity consumption fails to rise; it is that lethal heat rises faster than people’s capacity to pay for protection,” he added. Published in Dawn, July 29th, 2026

L'Europe confrontée à une nouvelle vague de chaleur, la climatisation au cœur du débat
items.description: L'Europe s'apprête à faire face à un nouvel épisode de chaleur extrême. À partir de ce mardi, plusieurs pays du continent devraient enregistrer des températures exceptionnellement élevées, quelques semaines seulement après une première vague de chaleur qui avait déjà affecté une large partie de l'Europe. Cette succession d'épisodes caniculaires intervient dans un contexte où les autorités sanitaires alertent sur l'intensification des effets du réchauffement climatique, marqué par des étés plus longs, plus chauds et des vagues de chaleur de plus en plus fréquentes. Les conséquences sanitaires de cette évolution préoccupent particulièrement l'Organisation mondiale de la santé (OMS). Selon l'agence onusienne, plus de 200.000 personnes ont perdu la vie en Europe au cours des quatre dernières années en raison des températures extrêmes. Sur les vingt dernières années, la mortalité liée à la chaleur a progressé d'environ 30 %. Pour le seul été en cours, les estimations préliminaires de l'OMS font état d'environ 10.000 décès supplémentaires imputables à la chaleur dans cinq pays européens. Si ce bilan reste provisoire, il témoigne néanmoins de l'ampleur des conséquences du changement climatique sur le continent. Les populations les plus vulnérables demeurent les personnes âgées, les enfants, les malades chroniques ainsi que les habitants de logements insuffisamment adaptés aux fortes chaleurs. Les épisodes caniculaires exercent également une pression croissante sur les systèmes de santé, avec une augmentation des admissions dans les services d'urgence et des difficultés, pour certains établissements hospitaliers, à maintenir des conditions d'accueil satisfaisantes durant les périodes de forte chaleur. L'OMS rappelle toutefois qu'une part importante de ces décès pourrait être évitée grâce à des politiques de prévention renforcées. L'organisation recommande notamment le développement des systèmes d'alerte précoce, le renforcement de la protection des populations les plus exposées, la création de davantage d'espaces verts ainsi qu'un meilleur accès à l'eau dans les zones régulièrement confrontées aux vagues de chaleur. La climatisation au cœur d'un débat européen La multiplication des épisodes de chaleur sur un continent qui se réchauffe à un rythme proche du double de la moyenne mondiale relance également le débat sur la place de la climatisation en Europe. Longtemps marginale dans une région habituée à des étés relativement tempérés, la climatisation est désormais perçue comme un moyen de protection face aux températures extrêmes, notamment pour les personnes les plus vulnérables. Son déploiement continue cependant de diviser. Certains y voient une réponse indispensable aux nouvelles conditions climatiques, tandis que d'autres mettent en avant ses conséquences sur la consommation d'énergie et son impact environnemental. En France, cette question s'est invitée dans les débats qui précèdent l'élection présidentielle de 2027. Les discussions portent notamment sur l'opportunité d'accélérer le recours à cette technologie ou, au contraire, de privilégier d'autres solutions telles que l'amélioration de l'isolation des bâtiments, le développement des espaces verts en milieu urbain ou encore une meilleure planification des villes. À ce jour, seuls environ 20 % des ménages européens sont équipés d'un système de climatisation, une proportion nettement inférieure à celle observée en Amérique du Nord ou dans plusieurs pays asiatiques. Cette situation pourrait toutefois évoluer rapidement. Selon des projections fondées sur les données de l'Agence internationale de l'énergie (AIE), le nombre d'unités de climatisation installées dans l'Union européenne pourrait atteindre 275 millions à l'horizon 2050, soit plus du double du niveau recensé en 2019. Les pays du sud de l'Europe, déjà confrontés à des étés particulièrement chauds, concentrent aujourd'hui la majorité de ces équipements. Cette tendance pourrait progressivement s'étendre à d'autres régions du continent à mesure que les épisodes de chaleur extrême deviennent plus fréquents. Adapter le continent à une nouvelle réalité climatique Cette évolution n'est toutefois pas sans conséquences. Les experts estiment qu'une généralisation de la climatisation entraînerait une forte hausse de la demande en électricité lors des pics de chaleur, alors même que les réseaux électriques sont soumis à de fortes contraintes. Elle pourrait également accroître les émissions de gaz à effet de serre si l'électricité consommée continue d'être produite à partir de sources fossiles. Le défi est d'autant plus important que l’empreinte carbone de l'Union européenne est estimée à environ neuf tonnes d'équivalent CO₂ par habitant et par an, contre une moyenne mondiale d'environ cinq tonnes. Face à des vagues de chaleur désormais plus fréquentes et plus intenses, l'Europe est appelée à revoir ses normes de construction, ses politiques urbaines et ses dispositifs de protection. Une grande partie du parc immobilier européen a en effet été conçue pour conserver la chaleur durant l'hiver, et non pour faire face aux températures estivales désormais observées. L'enjeu ne réside plus uniquement dans la gestion d'événements climatiques exceptionnels, mais dans l'adaptation durable du continent à des températures susceptibles de devenir la norme. Dans cette perspective, la future stratégie européenne de résilience face au changement climatique, attendue d'ici à la fin de l'année 2026, devrait constituer une nouvelle étape. Elle prévoit l'instauration d'un cadre commun destiné aux États membres, reposant sur des règles juridiquement contraignantes et des mécanismes de suivi visant à renforcer la coordination européenne face aux risques climatiques. The post L'Europe confrontée à une nouvelle vague de chaleur, la climatisation au cœur du débat appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Achakzai calls for Jirga on Balochistan security crisis
items.description: QUETTA: Opposition Leader in the National Assembly and Pakhtunkhwa Milli Awami Party (PkMAP) Chairman Mahmood Khan Achakzai has convened a three-day jirga in Quetta to discuss the worsening security situation in Balochistan and find solutions to the issue. He said the issue was becoming increasingly serious and dangerous with each passing day. Speaking at a press conference at the Quetta Press Club on Tuesday, along with other party leaders, he said the jirga would be held from August 29 to 31. He also announced that countrywide protest rallies and demonstrations would be held on August 5 to mark three years of imprisonment of former prime minister Imran Khan. He said the proposed jirga would bring together political leaders, tribal elders and other stakeholders to deliberate on rising insecurity, attacks on highways, disruption of trade, burning of goods vehicles and the killing of judges, lawyers, political workers and civilians in the province. He added that after discussions, the jirga would prepare recommendations on how to address the issue. Political leaders, tribal elders and stakeholders will participate in gathering to draft recommendations Achakzai, who is also chairman of the Tehreek-i-Tahaffuz Ayeen-i-Pakistan, expressed concern over the deteriorating law and order situation, alleging that frequent attacks had severely affected businesses and transport, leaving many people without livelihoods. He questioned what he described as the government’s failure to restore peace and ensure the protection of citizens’ lives, property and commercial activities. He also criticised what he termed the limited role of Parliament and provincial assemblies in addressing public concerns and alleged restrictions on the media’s ability to report freely. He condemned the killing of civilians in Kashmir and called for solidarity with the Kashmiri people. The PkMAP chief opposed the proposed division of districts in Balochistan’s Pashtun-majority areas, saying the move could create further complications. He announced that separate jirgas would also be convened to discuss administrative changes, with decisions to be made in consultation with local communities. Referring to attacks on transporters, Achakzai claimed that buses, trucks, oil tankers and other commercial vehicles belonging to Pashtuns had been targeted in Balochistan. He warned that transporters could suspend operations if such incidents continued and urged the government to ensure the safety of transport and trade routes. He also expressed concern over the killing of labourers in recent incidents and criticised the authorities’ handling of security-related events, including those in Hanna Urak and Ziarat. He qu­­estioned why no senior officials had been held accountable following the incidents. Achakzai further alleged that extortion was being demanded from drivers of goods vehicles travelling on national highways and called on the government and security institutions to take effective action against those responsible. He also criticised what he described as high airfares on flights between Quetta and Islamabad, saying they had become unaffordable for many passengers. Commenting on compensation for vehicles damaged in recent attacks, he said owners of 14 coal-laden trucks that were set on fire had each been offered Rs950,000, adding that affected transporters were demanding full compensation for their losses. Achakzai reiterated that political and security challenges could not be resolved through the use of force alone. He called for strengthening democratic institutions, an independent judiciary and a free media, saying lasting peace and stability could only be achieved through constitutional and democratic means. He also opposed the formation of tribal militias, arguing that maintaining law and order was the responsibility of state security institutions. Published in Dawn, July 29th, 2026

items.title: Indonesia: Environmentalists, Indigenous Leaders Unjustly Prosecuted
items.description: Click to expand Image An Indigenous Dayak villager shows pictures of her rubber plantation destroyed by an industrial logging company during a media interview in Sei Gawing village, Kapuas regency in Indonesia's Central Kalimantan Province, February 12, 2026. © 2026 BAY ISMOYO / AFP via Getty Images Indonesian authorities are wrongfully prosecuting environmental defenders who protest deforestation and pollution as well as Indigenous leaders who defend their land rights.The Prabowo administration has intensified the crackdown on free expression by expanding the military’s role in state-owned mining, oil palm plantations, infrastructure projects, and so-called food and energy estates.The government should fairly arbitrate disputes over land and environmental damage instead of punishing those who protest abuses. (Jakarta) – Indonesian authorities are pursuing wrongful prosecutions of environmentalists and Indigenous community leaders who protest deforestation and pollution, or defend land rights, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today. Since taking office in 2024, the administration of President Prabowo Subianto has intensified the crackdown on free expression by expanding the military’s role in state-owned mining, oil palm plantations, infrastructure projects, and so-called food and energy estates. The 70-page report, “Grabbed Land, Silenced Justice: The Persecution of Environmentalists and Indigenous Leaders in Indonesia,” documents how Indonesian police have responded to complaints filed by company officials or politicians by silencing Indigenous villagers who demand their customary land rights and the activists who defend them. The authorities have targeted environmental and Indigenous community defenders using the criminal code and other laws to bring charges ranging from defamation to “spreading communism” to silence protest over environmental harm. July 28, 2026 Grabbed Land, Silenced Justice The Persecution of Environmentalists and Indigenous Leaders in Indonesia Download the full report in English Download the Summary & Recommendations in Bahasa Indonesian Appendix: Letters to Indonesian Companies “Successive Indonesian governments have sought to silence activists and Indigenous leaders protesting forced displacement, loss of customary land, and deforestation by prosecuting them for baseless crimes,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The Prabowo government, while cracking down on corporate corruption, has ignored local community grievances and instead deployed the military and other heavy-handed measures to pursue its economic objectives.” Human Rights Watch examined more than 50 cases from 2015 to 2025 from the islands of Java, Sumatra, Kalimantan, Sulawesi, and the Moluccas, as well as the 6 provinces of Papua to select 15 high-profile cases as examples of specific laws and legal provisions used to target activists and community leaders, including in SLAPP (Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation) actions. The report is based on 69 interviews with villagers, Indigenous leaders, and environmental activists, as well as lawyers, academics, and government officials, and a review of police and court documents. The police and prosecutors have accused critics on slender evidence of Criminal Code offenses, Human Rights Watch found. In other cases, the authorities used provisions of the Plantation Law, the Mineral and Mining Law, the Job Creation Law, or the Prevention of Forest Destruction Law. While higher courts eventually rejected most cases, the targeted activists had to spend months rebutting baseless lawsuits. Haris Azhar, a human rights lawyer who was eventually acquitted of criminal defamation, said: “I had to spend time and energy overcoming attacks from the oligarchs and the police. I lost opportunities to build my advocacy work and to develop my professional career.” Indonesia is the world’s biggest producer of palm oil; a major gold, timber, paper and pulp producer; and the largest supplier of nickel, a key material for making steel and electric batteries. The Prabowo government has deployed the military to build “food and energy estates,” displacing local communities in South Papua. Since early 2025, the Prabowo government has seized control of plantations, mining sites, and other resource-rich land on corruption claims, and handed around six million hectares of oil palm plantations, among others, to state-owned companies. But some members of the government task force investigating the companies are themselves facing serious allegations of corruption. Under international human rights treaties that Indonesia has ratified, the government has the obligation to uphold the rights to life, liberty, speech, peaceful assembly, and association, among others. The duty to protect includes preventing corporations from committing abuses and taking steps to hold them accountable and provide reparation to victims when they do so. Business enterprises have a responsibility under the 2011 United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights to avoid causing or contributing to human rights abuses. Indonesia's government has drafted but not yet submitted legislation that would legally require companies operating in Indonesia to address the human rights impacts of their operations. The Prabowo administration should take steps to end the misuse of the Indonesian criminal justice system to harass, intimidate, and improperly punish environmentalists and Indigenous leaders, Human Rights Watch said. It should ensure prompt and equitable resolution of land conflicts between companies and local communities, especially in places such as Sumatra, Kalimantan, Sulawesi, the Moluccas Islands, and the six provinces of Papua. This includes restoring traditional ownership upon seizing illegal plantations and mining operations after consulting with the Registration of Indigenous Peoples, which has been mapping customary land rights. “The Indonesian government needs to make clear that arbitrarily dispossessing communities of their land is no longer business as usual,” Pearson said. “The authorities should fairly arbitrate disputes instead of punishing those who protest egregious abuses.” Selected Accounts Police arrested James Watt, an Indigenous Dayak farmer, who was living in Seruyan, Central Kalimantan, and championing sustainable agriculture in Jakarta on March 7, 2020, based on complaints by a company that the Dayak villagers had “harvested” palm fruits from a disputed 117-hectare site. Police also arrested two other farmers, Hermanus and Dilik. Hermanus died in police detention after being denied proper medical attention. On June 15, 2020, the Sampit district court found James Watt and Dilik guilty of stealing the oil palm fruits under the Plantation Law, sentencing James Watt to 10 months in prison and Dilik to 8 months. “The Indigenous community's rights were lost, and those who dared to question that decision were criminalized,” James Watt told Human Right Watch. “The governor [of Central Kalimantan] wrote a letter, declaring that those 117 hectares were outside the company’s HGU [right to use land]. His letter was simply ignored. The 10 months in prison is not a short time for me. The dramatic arrest in Jakarta, poor prison cells, and losing a friend [Hermanus], they all have a psychological impact. My good name, my time to be with my three children, my responsibility to find food for my family, to take care of my farm, these are losses that I must bear. They grabbed our lands, silenced those that sought justice. The injustice is clear.” Haslilin, a homemaker in Torobulu village, South Koname, Sulawesi Island, joined a protest against pollution caused by a nickel mining company on November 6, 2023. The villagers had repeatedly asked the company, as well as government officials, for the environmental impact assessment report (AMDAL), but their demands had gone unheeded. In March 2024, the police charged Haslilin and Andi Firmansyah, another villager, with “hindering” mining operations. On October 1, 2024, the Andoolo district court acquitted them, finding their assertion of a right to a healthy environment legitimate. “The company began to dig in 2021,” Haslilin said. “It was okay then, pretty far from the residential areas, but by 2023, it had become unbearable because they were digging very close to our houses. My youngest child has lung problems. Our water is polluted. We were curious how this could have happened and wanted to see their AMDAL [environment assessment report]. But they ignored us. So, I stopped the excavator, climbing the wheel and demanding that the operator show me the document. He did not have it. I was protesting because my village, my environment, is destroyed.” Police arrested Sorbatua Siallagan, an elder of the Indigenous Ompu Umbak Siallagan community in Simalungun, North Sumatra, on March 22, 2024, charging him with theft and arson, including burning eight eucalyptus trees belonging to a pulp and paper company. He was detained for seven months, and finally acquitted by the Supreme Court in June 2025. In January 2026, the Indonesian government revoked the company’s permits along with those of 27 others after authorities linked their alleged forest misuse to floods in Sumatra. Siallagan welcomed the government’s actions but said that the company’s security personnel still patrolled the overlapping territory. “They wouldn’t let us in” he said. “My friends were angry. The government should let the community return to their land, including for sacred rituals. We ask the government to truly return the land to us.” Villagers in the Tumpang Pitu area, Banyuwangi, East Java, organized a protest on April 4, 2017, outside the gate of a gold mining company they alleged had polluted the water, air, and soil, displaying protest banners. The company reported that one banner had a hammer and sickle. Police charged Heri Budiawan, nicknamed Budi Pego, a farmer involved in the protest, with “spreading communism.” On September 4, 2017, the Banyuwangi district court sentenced him to 10 months in prison. He appealed, saying that the banner, which was not presented in court, was not theirs. In October 2018, the Supreme Court upheld the decision, sentencing him to four years in prison. He was granted parole in November 2024. He said the villagers were continuing their fight but were demoralized. “I have concluded that it’s impossible to find the truth and to seek justice in Indonesia,” he said “The court has never presented that particular banner, only the photo. Our strength has been weakened.”

items.title: US walks out on France at UN Security Council
items.description: WASHINGTON: A rare public confrontation between two Western allies unfolded at the United Nations Security Council on Monday evening when the United States delegation walked out as the French ambassador began speaking. The dramatic gesture followed a sharp diplomatic exchange over human rights, the United Nations system and Washington’s decision to oppose the extension of the mandate of UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk. While Washington and Paris exchanged sharp accusations over human rights and the future of the UN system, Pakistan chose not to enter the dispute, focusing instead on the Ukraine war and the need for diplomacy. The US protest was triggered by criticism from France after a General Assembly vote on extending Turk’s four-year mandate. The resolution received overwhelming support, with 144 countries voting in favour. The United States was among only 10 countries that opposed the extension. Pakistan stays out of US-France dispute, focusing instead on Ukraine conflict Following the vote, France’s UN Mission in Geneva publicly criticised Washington’s position, saying: “The US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore.” The French statement also highlighted that the United States had voted against the resolution alongside countries including Russia and North Korea, a comparison that provoked an angry response from Washington. The Trump administration argued that the UN human rights system had become politically selective, accusing the High Commissioner’s office of focusing disproportionately on democratic countries such as the United States and Israel while failing to adequately challenge authoritarian governments. US Representative Jeff Bartos warned that the decision would have “consequences” and said it would lead to a broader reassessment of American funding for UN institutions. The dispute moved from public statements to the Security Council chamber. As French Ambassador Jerome Bonnafont took the floor, the American delegation staged a brief walkout in protest. After returning to the chamber, Alternate US Representative Dan Negrea sharply criticised the French comments, describing them as “disingenuous grandstanding” and “politicised drivel.” He said Washington would continue to skip French statements until Paris withdrew what he called “condescending and disrespectful rhetoric.” US Ambassador Mike Waltz also defended the move, accusing France of shifting attention away from its own decisions and claiming that Paris had chosen to “coddle some of the world’s worst human rights abusers” by supporting Turk’s reappointment. France, however, defended its position and the independence of the United Nations human rights system. Ambassador Bonnafont did not directly address the American walkout during his remarks. Instead, he emphasised the historic relationship between France and the United States, noting recent joint celebrations marking America’s 250th anniversary, while reiterating France’s commitment to maintaining an independent multilateral order. The clash reflected a wider disagreement between Washington and some of its traditional partners over the role of international institutions. Pakistan, meanwhile, maintained a careful distance from the confrontation. Speaking at the same Security Council meeting, Pakis­tan’s Ambassador to the United Nations, Asim Iftikhar Ahmad, focused entirely on the Ukraine war. Pakistan expressed “deep concern” over the continued escalation of the conflict, warning that attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure were causing an unacceptable humanitarian toll and affecting global food and energy security, particularly in developing countries. Published in Dawn, July 29th, 2026

items.title: FCC says earlier order in Imran’s release case remains in force
items.description: • Defers further hearing until after summer recess • Seeks replies in Radio Pakistan attack case ISLAMABAD: The Federal Consti­tutional Court (FCC) on Tuesday ruled that its earlier direction cautioning against any law and order situation in a case relating to the alleged mobilisation of the ‘ Imran Khan Release Force’ remains in force. A three-judge FCC bench, headed by Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan, made the observation after Advocate Ali Nawaz Kharral, counsel for petitioner Malik Zaheer Ahmed, requested the court to extend its earlier order, expressing apprehensions that the respondents might create a law and order situation. Responding to the request, the chief justice observed that the respondents would not do so and clarified that the earlier directions were not limited to Tuesday’s hearing but continued to remain effective. The FCC is hearing a petition filed by Malik Zaheer Ahmed, who challenged the legal status of the movement, arguing that the formation of a force to secure the release of jailed PTI founder Imran Khan violated the Constitution and posed a threat to public order. At the outset of the hearing, Advocate Ali Bukhari, appearing for PTI leaders, sought time to submit a power of attorney and a reply on behalf of PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja. The counsel informed the court that, besides representing Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, he had also been engaged that morning to represent the PTI secretary general. He requested additional time to file a reply, describing the petition as politically motivated. The court accepted the request and adjourned further proceedings until after the summer vacation. KP chief minister’s response On Monday, the KP chief minister submitted a reply categorically denying the existence of any armed structure or paramilitary setup. He maintained that the Imran Khan Rehayi Aman Movement was a peaceful, unarmed and voluntary civic initiative aimed at raising awareness about due process of law. The response stated that the alleged Imran Khan Rehai Force had neither been constituted, notified nor operationalised at any stage, and that no armed structure, organisational militancy, coercive framework or paramilitary setup existed or had ever been contemplated. It further argued that any earlier reference to the term “force”, if misunderstood, had no legal or factual basis. According to the reply, the initiative was a peaceful political movement intended to promote awareness of due process and the state’s responsibility to ensure fairness in criminal prosecutions. In his petition, Malik Zaheer Ahmed argued that the chief minister’s announcement regarding the proposed force violated the constitutional oath he took as an MPA and chief minister. He contended that, although no such force had been formally established, the public announcement of its proposed formation and mobilisation had created fear, uncertainty and unrest among the public. Radio Pakistan attack case In a separate case, the same bench directed the respondents to file concise statements within two weeks in a petition relating to the May 10, 2023, attack on Radio Pakistan Peshawar, in which Chief Minister Sohail Afridi is among the accused. The court also ordered that its earlier stay restraining the Special Judge of the Anti-Terrorism Court-III, Peshawar, from proceeding with the trial would continue. The stay was granted on a petition filed by the Pakistan Broadcasting Corporation (PBC), which sought the transfer of the criminal case from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to an anti-terrorism court in Islamabad or another province, citing alleged political pressure and executive interference that had undermined the prospects of a fair trial. Notices had earlier been issued to 84 respondents. Published in Dawn, July 29th, 2026

items.title: SHO among 11 cops booked over raid on AGP Mansoor Awan's house in Lahore
items.description: LAHORE: Eleven police officials, including the station house officer (SHO) of Sarwar Road police station, have been booked and charge-sheeted after they allegedly raided the residence of Attorney General for Pakistan Mansoor Awan in Lahore and harassed household staff, exceeding their lawful authority. According to the police, the SHO, Irfan, has obtained interim bail from a court. According to the FIR, a police party led by Sarwar Road SHO entered the attorney general’s residence at around 6pm on July 27 after scaling the main gate. The officials allegedly harassed employees present in the house and damaged flower pots placed outside the residence during the operation. At the time of the police raid, the attorney general was away, attending a meeting and returned home after being informed of the incident. The police say the raid was conducted on a tip-off about the alleged presence of some suspects in a neighbouring house, but the raiding team mistakenly entered the residence of the attorney general. The FIR further states that the police officials exceeded their authority while conducting the raid, prompting registration of a criminal case and initiation of departmental proceedings against them by issuing charge sheets. The attorney general’s driver, Irfan, alleged that the police team also took away the house’s CCTV recording system. He claimed the footage of the raid was deleted before the digital video recorder (DVR) was returned. Further legal and departmental proceedings are underway. Published in Dawn, July 29th, 2026

items.title: Rivers may swell again as fresh monsoon spell arrives
items.description: • Met Office predicts rain across country from today until Aug 5; warns of likely flash floods, landslides • Indus in medium-flood at Guddu, eastern rivers may surge amid fresh spell • Rescue efforts continue as villages on Lahore outskirts remain submerged • PM reviews monsoon response LAHORE/RAWALPINDI: With another torrential spell of monsoon rains expected from July 29, the water level in the Indus River on Tuesday was steadily increasing, with the river likely to experience a medium-level flood at Guddu Barrage within 24 hours (Wednesday evening), while flooding in the Ravi and Chenab rivers had reduced considerably. According to an irrigation official in Punjab, the situation in the eastern rivers had improved, but the looming monsoon spell in the catchment areas could increase their flow again. From July 29 to Aug 5, almost all parts of the country will receive heavy rains, which may generate flash floods in hilly regions and inundate urban centres, prompting the prime minister to chair a meeting on preparations ahead of the deluge. The Flood Forecasting Division warned that the rainfall forecast from July 30 onwards in the upper catchment areas could increase water flows in the eastern rivers and their adjoining hill torrents. It added that a rise in flows was also expected in tributaries of the Kabul River, as well as hill torrents in the Dera Ghazi Khan Division and northeastern Balochistan. The flows in the eastern rivers (Sutlej, Ravi and Beas) and associated tributaries were also expected to rise from July 30 to August 4. Rainfall across country The Pakistan Meteorological Department said the new spell could generate flash floods in local streams in Kashmir, Murree, Galiyat, northeastern Punjab, Islamabad, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Gilgit-Baltistan, hill torrents of Dera Ghazi Khan, and northeastern parts of Balochistan. The Met office said that monsoon currents from the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal were likely to penetrate the upper and central parts of the country from today. According to the PMD, heavy rains may cause urban flooding in the low-lying areas of Islamabad, Rawalpindi, Peshawar, Nowshera, Gujranwala, Gujrat, Sialkot, Lahore, Multan and Faisalabad from July 30 to August 4. In Sindh’s Nawabshah, Sukkur, Shaheed Benazirabad, Hyderabad, Thatta, Badin, Sanghar, Khairpur, Mithi, Mirpur Khas, Umerkot, Tando Muhammad Khan, Tando Allahyar districts, urban flooding is expected from July 31 to August 2. Dir, Chitral, Swat, Kohistan, Buner, Battagram, Mansehra, Haripur, Abbottabad, Gilgit-Baltistan, Murree, Galiyat, and Kashmir can experience landslides from July 30 to August 5 due to the downpour, which would also flood local streams and hill torrents in Balochistan, GB, KP and southern Punjab. River flows In its Tuesday evening forecast, the division stated that the Indus river, in the next 24 hours, was likely to attain a medium-level flood at Guddu Barrage, while at Sukkur Barrage it was expected to flow at a low-flood level. Similarly, Chashma and Sukkur barrages were likely to experience low-level flooding, while Kalabagh Barrage was expected to continue recording low flood levels. The FFD said that Head Panjnad was likely to enter the low-flood category, whereas the flood at the Balloki and Sulemanki barrages was expected to remain in the low category. According to the FFD, the River Ravi at Sidhnai was likely to enter the medium flood category, whereas the Jhelum and Chenab were likely to enter the below-low flood level category at Mangla, Rasul, Marala, Khanki, Qadirabad and Trimmu. According to a daily water report issued by the Water and Power Development Authority (Wapda), the inflows and outflows in the Indus at Tarbela were recorded as 242,900 cusecs and 189,300 cusecs, respectively, followed by the River Kabul at Nowshera, which had inflows of 49,100 cusecs and outflows of 49,100 cusecs. The Jhelum at Mangla had inflows of 48,500 cusecs and outflows of 86,000 cusecs, and the Chenab at Marala had inflows of 89,600 cusecs and outflows of 78,400 cusecs. Flooded villages The irrigation official said flooded nullahs, which had to be breached during the recent floods, submerged large tracts of land along the GT Road near Lahore and Gujranwala, besides Kasur. AFP from Muridke reported that floodwaters spread across fields and villages near Muridke. “Floodwater has inundated our area since Friday, leaving the entire neighbourhood submerged,” said Muhammad Faisal, 39, a labourer. Haris Dar, a rescue volunteer, said dozens of villages remained under water and teams were continuing to evacuate stranded residents while distributing meals to affected families. A statement issued after the PM-led meeting claimed that in some areas, agricultural land had been inundated due to floods in seasonal streams, and drainage operations were underway. According to the statement, 110 people have lost their lives, 360 people have been injured, 796 houses have been damaged, and 376 heads of livestock have perished during the ongoing monsoon season. PM chairs meeting The meeting chaired by PM Shehbaz Sharif on the ongoing monsoon rains and floods across the country directed all authorities to be prepared to meet any emergency. According to the PM’s Office, the premier directed the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) to remain in constant coordination with the provincial disaster management authorities (PDMAs) and the provincial governments. The prime minister also directed Federal Minister for Planning Ahsan Iqbal to chair the flood committee’s meetings on a daily basis and determine the appropriate course of action after reviewing the evolving situation. He said the government was rapidly implementing short-, medium-, and long-term measures to address the impacts of climate change. Officials of the NDMA and chief secretaries told the briefing that 700 locations had been identified across the country to store rainwater during monsoon. Syed Irfan Raza in Islamabad also contributed to this report Published in Dawn, July 29th, 2026

Nationwide iPhone scam probe widens
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Federal Tax Ombudsman (FTO) has detected what it termed an organised scam involving the import and clearance of an iPhone 16 and directed the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) to investigate the alleged role of FedEx, Customs officials and private individuals to determine whether similar frauds have occurred across the country. Federal Tax Ombudsman Zafar Hijazi in his order released on Tuesday observed that the case pointed to a coordinated scheme through which a lawful consignee was deprived of his duty-paid mobile phone for more than one-and-a-half years despite paying all applicable taxes. The complaint was filed by Muhammad Nausherwan Khan, who stated that his sister in Canada sent him an iPhone 16 Plus through FedEx in December 2024. After the handset arrived in Karachi, he paid the PTA tax of Rs138,526 but alleged that the phone was never delivered to him. He later discovered that a forged authority letter had allegedly been used to release the device to another person. During the proceedings, Customs maintained that the mobile phone had been released after verifying the original detention receipt, invoice and other documents presented by a clearing agent. However, the Ombudsman questioned why the complainant, whose name appeared as the consignee on the import documents, was denied possession despite personally approaching Customs authorities. FTO orders inquiry into courier fraud allegations The FTO found that while the consignee’s name remained unchanged in the tracking records and import documents, the address and contact details had allegedly been substituted with those of another individual in the airway bill and invoice. The Ombudsman observed that such manipulation was indicative of an organised scam and stated that the modus operandi could not be ignored. Although the complainant subsequently informed the Ombudsman that his grievance had been resolved, the FTO decided to continue pursuing the broader issue, saying the suspected scam required a thorough investigation to protect the public interest. The Ombudsman recommended that FBR direct the Chief Collector of Customs (Airports) to initiate a targeted inquiry into FedEx, obtain courier import data for January 2025-June 2026 to identify similar cases, investigate the alleged use of forged authority letters, examine the role of Customs officials who may have facilitated the scam, and initiate legal and disciplinary proceedings where warranted. The FTO also recommended introducing a uniform standard operating procedure for courier clearances at all international airports. Published in Dawn, July 29th, 2026

items.title: Power division pins blame for circular debt on ‘Q Block’
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The power division on Tuesday blamed the Ministry of Finance for a Rs61 billion increase in power sector circular debt, which rose to Rs1.675 trillion by June 30 this year from Rs1.614tr a year earlier. “Due to the budget deduction of Rs98bn, the circular debt witnessed an increase of Rs61bn” during FY2025-26, the power division said in a statement. It did not release the end-year financial report, which is pending regulatory and statutory approval. As such, the power sector circular debt, excluding K-Electric, concluded the fiscal year at Rs1.675tr. Under the International Monetary Fund programme, the government has committed to no increase in circular debt flow and a gradual reduction in its stock. The end-December 2025 target under the programme was met and appreciated by the IMF. The power division said a total of Rs893bn was allocated for the power sector in the federal budget for FY26. “However, a deduction of Rs98bn was subsequently made. Had the power sector received the full allocated budgetary payment, the circular debt would have further reduced to Rs1.577tr,” it said. Budget documents presented to parliament showed that Rs1.036tr was actually allocated for power sector subsidies, which was later reduced to Rs893bn at the time of presentation of the FY27 budget. The power division statement, however, indicated that a further Rs98bn cut was imposed as part of the austerity policy before the current-year budget was passed, effectively reducing the power sector subsidy to Rs795bn. The statement recalled that the power sector’s circular debt had decreased from Rs2.393tr in FY24 to Rs1.614tr in FY25. It said losses of power distribution companies, which stood at Rs591bn in FY24, were reduced by Rs193bn to Rs397bn in FY25. “During the current fiscal year, the power division has further reduced these losses from Rs397bn to Rs326bn,” it said, adding that over a two-year period, overall losses were curtailed by Rs265bn, bringing them down from Rs591bn to Rs326bn. “This reduction clearly demonstrates that the reforms implemented in the power sector are proving effective and yielding sustained positive outcomes,” the power division claimed. It added that the numbers confirmed that the reform process within the energy sector was progressing effectively. The division said the budget deduction was merely a temporary financial factor rather than a reflection of any operational decline. It said it remained committed to executing its reform agenda to ensure that the energy sector became financially sustainable and reliable for consumers. Published in Dawn, July 29th, 2026

items.title: UN chief condemns Israeli settler violence in West Bank
items.description: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has condemned the attacks by Israeli settlers in the West Bank, including arson attacks on two mosques, his deputy spokesperson said on Tuesday. "The secretary-general condemns the attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank, including the reported arson attacks on two mosques, vandalism of private property, and attacks targeting Palestinians and their livelihoods," his deputy spokesperson Farhan Haq said. "Attacks against places of worship are heinous and unacceptable and risk further inflaming an already volatile situation," Haq said. "The secretary-general calls for those responsible to be swiftly identified and held accountable, in line with Israel's obligations under international law." Guterres further calls on the Israeli authorities to take immediate and effective measures to prevent further attacks by settlers against Palestinians and their property, including places of worship, and to ensure the protection of civilians, Haq said. The secretary-general urges all parties to exercise maximum restraint, prevent any further escalation, and take immediate steps to restore calm and reduce tensions, the spokesperson said. A new wave of settler violence broke out last week in the West Bank. Violent incidents southwest of Nablus on July 24 resulted in the killing of four Palestinians and two Israelis, injuries to several others and extensive damage to Palestinian property, UN Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process Ramiz Alakbarov told the Security Council on Tuesday. Following the incidents near Nablus, Israel launched a large-scale arrest campaign in the West Bank, detaining at least 80 Palestinians. On July 26, Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian villages in the West Bank and set fire to two mosques – one south of Nablus and the other south of Tulkarm, according to press reports.

items.title: Brunei's sultan meets with Chinese defense minister
items.description: Brunei's Sultan Haji Hassanal Bolkiah Mu'izzaddin Waddaulah met with visiting Chinese Defense Minister Dong Jun on Tuesday. Hassanal reaffirmed Brunei's firm commitment to the one-China policy, expressed appreciation for China's support for ASEAN centrality, and extended thanks to China for its assistance to Brunei's efforts to realize its national vision, Wawasan 2035. Emphasizing that defense cooperation serves as a key pillar of the two countries' strategic cooperative partnership, he said Brunei looks forward to more port calls by the Chinese Navy. For his part, Dong noted that China-Brunei military cooperation now faces important development opportunities, urging the two sides to build on the positive momentum to elevate all-dimensional cooperation, and deliver more tangible outcomes to contribute to building a China-Brunei community with a shared future and opening new prospects for bilateral relations. Stressing that peace in the South China Sea bears on the common interests of all regional countries, Dong said that China stands ready to strengthen practical cooperation with Brunei in maritime security and other relevant fields to jointly safeguard peace and stability in the region.

items.title: Govt increases petrol price by Rs1.63, HSD price by Rs1.55
items.description: Pakistan fuel prices, 2026 Official ex-depot prices (PKR/litre) — OGRA & Ministry of Energy notifications Petrol (MS-92) Diesel (HSD) Pre-crisis baseline Source: OGRA / Ministry of Energy (Petroleum Division); Dawn.com · "> The government on Tuesday increased the prices of petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs1.63 and Rs1.55 per litre, respectively, passing on the impact of fluctuating global oil prices after hostilities flared again in the Persian Gulf earlier this month. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs335.81 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs388.38 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs110 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs96 per litre on diesel. The Petroleum Division’s notification said the new prices would be applicable for July 29 (Wednesday). The diesel price has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Earlier, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. The government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. The daily pricing decision was rejected by the All Pakistan Dealers Association, which said it would consider a protest plan this week. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

items.title: Accidents de la circulation : 30 morts et 3.026 blessés en périmètre urbain du 20 au 26 juillet
items.description: Trente personnes ont trouvé la mort et 3.026 autres ont été blessées, dont 125 grièvement, dans 2.208 accidents de la circulation survenus en périmètre urbain durant la semaine allant du 20 au 26 juillet, selon la Direction Générale de la Sûreté Nationale (DGSN). Ces accidents sont principalement dus à l'inadvertance des conducteurs, au non-respect de la priorité, à la non maîtrise du véhicule, à l'inadvertance des piétons, à l'excès de vitesse, au changement de direction non autorisé, au non-respect de la distance de sécurité, au changement de direction sans usage du clignotant, au non-respect du feu rouge, au non-respect du stop, à la circulation sur la voie gauche, à la circulation en sens interdit, à la conduite en état d’ébriété et au dépassement défectueux, précise la DGSN dans un communiqué. Concernant les opérations de contrôle et de répression en matière de circulation, les services de sûreté ont enregistré 49.357 contraventions, dressé 7.659 procès-verbaux transmis au Parquet et procédé au recouvrement de 41.698 amendes transactionnelles. Les sommes perçues au titre de ces contraventions ont atteint 9.208.075 dirhams, ajoute le communiqué qui fait état de la mise en fourrière municipale de 5.031 véhicules, de la saisie de 7.659 documents et du retrait de la circulation de 420 véhicules. The post Accidents de la circulation : 30 morts et 3.026 blessés en périmètre urbain du 20 au 26 juillet appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Saving tigers means saving ecosystems
items.description: International Tiger Day, observed on July 29, highlights how tiger conservation is increasingly focused not only on recovering populations but also on restoring the ecosystems that sustain them. Spanning 14,100 square kilometers, the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park is home to around 72 wild Siberian tigers, making it one of the species' most important strongholds in China. Supported by an integrated monitoring system combining camera traps, satellite remote sensing and aerial surveys, AI-powered stripe-pattern recognition helps researchers identify individual tigers and track their movements, while long-term monitoring provides valuable data for conservation planning. Its approach reflects a broader shift from protecting individual animals to conserving the ecosystems they depend on. That approach mirrors a global trend. According to World Wildlife Fund, an estimated 5,574 wild tigers remain worldwide today, up significantly from an estimated 3,200 in 2010. Much of the recovery has been reported in India, Nepal and Bhutan, while Russia and China have also recorded population recovery. Populations in parts of Southeast Asia, however, continue to face severe pressure from habitat loss, poaching and human-wildlife conflict. The next challenge is no longer increasing tiger numbers, but reconnecting fragmented habitats and improving coexistence between people and wildlife. Earlier this year, the International Union for Conservation of Nature announced six initiatives across Bhutan, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Nepal and Thailand that combine habitat restoration, wildlife corridors, community participation and conflict mitigation. Rather than focusing on protected areas alone, the projects aim to reconnect forests across national boundaries and strengthen connected ecosystems. A recent study published in the Frontiers in Conservation Science journal likewise argues that long-term tiger recovery depends on maintaining ecological connectivity and integrating conservation with local livelihoods. China's efforts are also extending beyond its borders. In 2024, China and Russia agreed to establish the "Land of Big Cats," a transboundary conservation area linking about 18,000 square kilometers of tiger and leopard habitat. In Kazakhstan, Siberian tigers were released this year as part of an internationally supported effort to restore tigers to parts of their former range, where the Caspian tiger became extinct decades ago. These initiatives show how tiger conservation is evolving from protecting a single species to safeguarding the connected landscapes on which both wildlife and people depend. For more: Uniting for tigers: A global conservation initiative

items.title: 13 dead after powerful quake strikes Japan's Kumamoto
items.description: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on Wednesday that 13 people had been confirmed dead after a powerful earthquake struck Kumamoto Prefecture in southwestern Japan. The magnitude-7.1 quake struck Kumamoto Prefecture at 4:27 p.m. on Tuesday (1927 GMT) at a depth of about 10 kilometers, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency. According to the Kumamoto prefectural government, eight people had been pulled out from inside AEON Mall Kumamoto, a major shopping complex in Kashima Town in the region. Among them, two women in their 20s were confirmed dead, while another person was found in cardiac arrest. Authorities are investigating a possible gas explosion, local media reported. The full extent of the disaster remained unclear. Around 20 to 30 mall workers were unaccounted for on Tuesday, NHK said. The earthquake caused widespread damage, with houses, factories and other buildings collapsing in the affected area. Seven people are also missing after a chimney collapsed at a Nippon Paper Industries factory, while four others are seriously injured, a local government official said. The earthquake has also severely disrupted transport infrastructure in the area. Rail services across Kyushu, including the Kyushu Shinkansen, have been suspended. NHK reported damage to a viaduct in Yatsushiro, Kumamoto Prefecture. Across the prefecture, which also suffered a deadly earthquake a decade ago, around 260,000 people were instructed to go to evacuation centers, authorities said. The quake's epicenter was about 20 kilometers (12 miles) south ‌of Kumamoto City, central Kyushu's largest city with a population of around 700,000. Authorities have warned residents in the areas that felt the biggest tremors to be on alert for ​further strong quakes for about a week, as well as for the risk of landslides. With more than 36,000 homes still without power, authorities are worried about the risk of heat stroke as temperatures soar to around 34 degrees Celsius on Wednesday. (With input from Reuters)

items.title: The American Commentator Making Excuses for Iran
items.description: When I saw that the commentator Max Blumenthal was going to speak in Washington, D.C., about his recent trip to Iran, I couldn’t stay away. I have long been fascinated with Americans—especially privileged, well-connected Americans—who, out of alienation from their own country, show an admiration for distant authoritarian lands. Blumenthal, the son of the Clinton-family adviser and former journalist Sidney Blumenthal, was one of some 400 pro-regime influencers invited by the Iranian government to cover the funeral earlier this month of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in a joint U.S.-Israeli air strike on February 28. Speaking last week at the flagship location of the progressive bookstore and restaurant chain Busboys and Poets, Blumenthal portrayed the man who’d overseen the mass slaughter of young Iranian protesters in January as “a father, a guide, a religious teacher” and presented the regime that he’d led as not only legitimate but also an inspiration to the world. Khamenei’s assassination, he told the standing-room-only crowd, ought to have generated far more outrage than it did. “Imagine,” he said, “if a rogue foreign state went and assassinated the pope, how so many Catholics would feel.” The analogy feels slightly off: Pontiffs aren’t typically known for brandishing rifles at Mass or calling for the death of entire countries . [ Graeme Wood: The U.S. is subtly shifting its Iran strategy ] Blumenthal has become part of an ignominious tradition. In the early 1930s, the Pulitzer Prize–winning New York Times correspondent Walter Duranty wrote stories denying the famine that Joseph Stalin’s forced-collectivization policies were causing in Ukraine and mocked journalists who reported the truth. “Russians Hungry, but Not Starving,” read the headline of one Duranty dispatch, which repeated an insouciant justification of revolutionary violence: “You can’t make an omelette without breaking eggs.” Blumenthal doesn’t have the prestige of the newspaper of record behind him. But illustrious affiliations are no longer necessary to gain an audience. On X, Blumenthal has nearly 860,000 followers. He appears regularly on Russian , Chinese , Turkish , Iranian , and Venezuelan state-funded media. He founded a website, The Grayzone, whose roster of contributors includes alumni of Kremlin-backed media outlets . (Blumenthal did not respond to a request for comment for this article.) On multiple platforms, Blumenthal has vouched for the world’s worst mass murderers. At Russia’s invitation, Blumenthal addressed the United Nations Security Council, where he denounced Ukraine and described Western support for it as an “international Ponzi scheme.” He denied that deposed Syrian President Bashar al-Assad used chemical weapons against his own people and has implied that Syrian rebels did. He denied Hamas’s systemic sexual violence against Israeli women on October 7. “A Chinese state media darling,” according to Axios , Blumenthal has downplayed evidence that the Chinese government is repressing its Uyghur Muslim minority. Outside Busboys and Poets before Blumenthal’s talk, two young Iranian women held a banner commemorating the demonstrators who had been killed by forces of the Islamic Republic during two days of protests in January. On his way into the store, Blumenthal paused to berate them . “Zionist cuck,” “Sellouts,” and “Persian gusanas ,” he shouted at them. ( Gusanas is the feminine form of the Spanish word for “worms”—what Fidel Castro called Cubans who fled his dictatorship.) When Blumenthal entered the venue, he received rapturous applause. Sitting on a stage beneath portraits of the Dalai Lama, Mahatma Gandhi, and Martin Luther King Jr., he began with a breakdown of “Operation Epstein Fury,” a nod to the claim that President Trump initiated the war against Iran to distract the American people from his connection to the deceased financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. But the actual instigator of the conflict, Blumenthal explained, was Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, America’s “real president,” who’d visited the White House Situation Room in February and taken “the unprecedented step of sitting at the head of the table, moving Donald Trump to the side.” (The most detailed account of the meeting, by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan of The New York Times , placed Netanyahu on a side of the table, opposite Trump). It was at this meeting, according to Blumenthal, that Israel (“the epicenter of evil in the world”) ordered the United States (“the most perfidious force on the planet”) to attack Iran. Blumenthal presents himself as a courageous truth teller whose work is too daring for the corporate media. But mainstream outlets abound with criticism of every aspect of the war, including Israel’s role in it. Indeed, outside the precincts of Trump-friendly media, the daily coverage of the conflict has been almost uniformly negative. But there’s a market for a darker and more insidious explanation as to how the world works. Blumenthal delivered just that—a conspiratorial account of Jewish power, American malignity, and the Islamic Republic’s righteousness. When he mentioned mourners at Khamenei’s funeral holding signs declaring KILL TRUMP , a smattering of applause broke out. Blumenthal then returned to the country that Iranian leaders call “the Little Satan.” “Do we actually believe that the U.S. would be attacking Iran right now if Israel did not have full control over the Trump administration?” Blumenthal asked. He insinuated that Miriam Adelson, a Jewish Republican donor, had bribed the president to attack Iran, and he accused the Jewish state of trying to “weaponize the assassination attempts to manipulate Trump.” Israel would be “indirectly responsible” for an Iranian attempt on Trump’s life, which would be “blowback for the special relationship with Israel.” In other words, anything that happened to the president would be Israel’s fault. Assessing the real motives and intentions of the regime in Tehran is difficult. Because Iran is a theocratic dictatorship that routinely arrests and in some cases executes journalists, Western reporters hoping to cover the country must either work clandestinely or submit to government supervision. Blumenthal sneered at his mainstream-media colleagues who disclosed in their stories that they were reporting from Iran with the Iranian government’s permission. “So they’re basically trying to say Iran is this authoritarian country that controls their coverage,” he argued. Blumenthal also defended the regime’s monitoring of foreign journalists due to “the long history of U.S. surveillance and spying and sabotaging.” Jason Rezaian, the Washington Post reporter who was convicted on phony espionage charges and jailed for 544 days , might beg to differ with Blumenthal’s analysis. In defending the Islamic Republic, Blumenthal made one false or misleading assertion after another. He parroted the regime’s claim that 35 million people had participated in Khamenei’s funeral, “possibly the largest gathering in human history.” He said that women make up a greater percentage of the Iranian Parliament than the U.S. Congress. (In reality, only 5 percent of members of the Majlis are women, compared with more than a quarter of Congress.) He described Israel’s apparently unintentional bombing of a Tehran synagogue as a deliberate act; the presence of a captive Jewish community in Iran “discredits Zionism,” by Blumenthal’s account. The exile-staffed news network Iran International, he said without evidence, is “run by Israeli intelligence,” and “there is so much U.S. air power concentrated in Israel right now that Israel will not allow U.S. planes to be at Ben Gurion International.” In reality, the Tel Aviv airport has bent over backwards to accommodate the U.S. Air Force, at one point reducing its civilian flight capacity to about a third of normal. Blumenthal was particularly keen to minimize the Iranian regime’s brutality toward its own people. The regime maintains that slightly more than 3,000 people were killed during January’s anti-government protests, which Blumenthal characterized as “riots.” Reporting by human-rights groups and other journalists tells a different story. According to Time , so many people were killed during the two days of protest that “the state’s capacity to dispose of the dead” was “overwhelmed.” Two senior health-ministry officials, speaking anonymously, told the magazine that at least 30,000 dead (and possibly many more) was a likelier figure, and one that was corroborated by a group of first responders who collected data surreptitiously. Blumenthal insisted that a death toll this high isn’t possible. Regime opponents’ estimates of 40,000 or more dead, he said, are “fake numbers.” Blumenthal was most contemptuous toward Iranians who do not share his rosy view of the late ayatollah and the brutal theocracy that he led for nearly four decades. He described Masih Alinejad, the Iranian exile whom the regime brazenly tried to murder in Brooklyn and who wears a flower in her hair in protest of the forced hijab, as “basically a CIA asset” and “the lady with the hair.” Her flower, he said, “should be drenched in blood.” Blumenthal showed no patience for Iranians he met who blame their government’s economic mismanagement, and not America, for their troubles. “I mean, as ignorant as you think Americans are about sanctions, there are many Iranians who don’t really see the role of sanctions in their economic misery,” he complained. Presidents of both parties have provided critics of American foreign policy with endless grounds for legitimate criticism. But the work of Blumenthal and others like him reveals a reflexive paranoia, if not hatred, of the United States and its allies, to the point where criticism is insufficient. Far too often, they veer into downplaying or even endorsing the depravities of illiberal governments and movements simply because they adopt an “anti-imperialist” posture. Sadly, there is a large and growing audience for this reactionary analysis. “One of the reasons why I opened Busboys and Poets is to educate people,” the chain’s owner, Andy Shallal, said before Blumenthal took the stage. Shallal extolled the importance of freedom of speech, freedom of expression, international law, and international norms. These are fine principles, the bedrock of any decent society. What’s jarring is to hear them invoked on behalf of someone doing public relations for a regime that flouts every one of them.
